articles.title: British sisters lose £90 million legal battle against LOL Surprise maker MGA Entertainment after court rejects their claim over alleged threats to major UK toy retailers stocking rival Worldeez toys
articles.summary: Two British sisters have lost a major court battle against US toy giant MGA Entertainment after seeking up to £90 million in damages over claims that the
articles.body: Two British sisters have lost a major court battle against US toy giant MGA Entertainment after seeking up to £90 million in damages over claims that the company deliberately sabotaged their collectable toy brand, Worldeez. Hayley Michaelson and Lauren Cohen alleged that MGA threatened to withdraw its popular LOL Surprise products from major UK retailers if they stocked their competing toy. Although the High Court previously found that MGA had engaged in an unlawful campaign to exclude Worldeez from the market, it refused to award compensation, ruling that the business would not have traded profitably anyway. The Court of Appeal has now dismissed the sisters' challenge.How did the British sisters come up with the idea for Worldeez toysThe idea for Worldeez emerged during a family holiday in 2014, when sisters Hayley Michaelson and Lauren Cohen, alongside their husbands Marc Michaelson and Johnny Cohen, discussed creating a collectable toy inspired by children's interest in unboxing videos and surprise toys.The product was designed as a globe-shaped capsule containing country-themed collectables. Its initial range covered eight countries, including the UK, France, Italy, Brazil, India, Egypt, Japan and the US, with 15 figurines for each country. The business secured investment and planned to distribute the toys through major retailers Smyths, Toys 'R' Us and The Entertainer.How did the Worldeez toy brand lose major UK retail dealsAccording to evidence presented during the appeal, Cabo's barrister Stefan Kupper said MGA began its campaign on 23 May 2017, after seeing a YouTube video featuring child influencer Tiana promoting Worldeez. He alleged that the company threatened to withhold supplies of its popular LOL Surprise collectables from retailers that agreed to stock the competing product.The allegations also included claims that MGA repeatedly described Worldeez as a 'knock-off' and threatened legal action over alleged intellectual property and patent infringement. According to Mr Kupper, The Entertainer subsequently cancelled an order it had placed, while Smyths and Toys 'R' Us did not proceed with orders. Worldeez eventually reached the market through discount retailer B&M, but its initial sales declined.Why did the judge refuse to award damages to the Worldeez foundersCabo previously brought the dispute before the High Court, where Mrs Justice Bacon found that MGA had used coercive tactics against three major UK toy retailers as part of an overall campaign to exclude Worldeez. The judge concluded that the threats to withdraw LOL Surprise supplies, alongside the legal threats and allegations of imitation, amounted to an abuse of a dominant market position.However, the judge refused to award damages, finding that Cabo would not have traded profitably even without MGA's conduct. She acknowledged that Worldeez was an appealing product with an initially successful online marketing campaign, but said it was competing in a crowded collectables market and needed more than that to succeed.What arguments did both sides present in the Worldeez Court of Appeal battleCabo subsequently appealed the decision, arguing that the High Court had placed an unfair burden on a start-up business by requiring it to demonstrate that it would have been profitable in circumstances where its launch had allegedly been prevented. Mr Kupper argued that the company's lost opportunity to secure distribution through major retailers had caused it harm.Representing MGA, barrister Victoria Wakefield KC disputed the appeal, arguing that Cabo was seeking to establish an open-ended damages award despite the finding that it would not have been profitable in the alternative circumstances. She also challenged the company's original claim of up to £90 million. Following a two-day hearing in London, Lord Justice Males, Lord Justice Popplewell and Lord Justice Phillips dismissed Cabo's appeal. The judges said their reasons for the decision would be provided at a later date.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: PM Modi to attend Asean, East Asia summits in Manila; what's on agenda
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi will travel to Manila on Monday for a two-day visit to attend the 23rd India-Asean Summit and the 21st East Asia
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi will travel to Manila on Monday for a two-day visit to attend the 23rd India-Asean Summit and the 21st East Asia Summit. Maritime security, regional stability and expanding trade ties are expected to be key focus areas at the meetings.Announcing his visit to Manila, PM Modi said in a post on X, "Will be in Manila, Philippines later today and tomorrow to attend the following programmes: 23rd Asean-India Summit. 21st East Asia Summit.""India attaches immense importance to close friendship with Asean nations. I’m also looking forward to interacting with the Indian community based in the Philippines," he added.The visit comes as India seeks to strengthen its strategic engagement with Southeast Asia amid rapid geopolitical changes in the Indo-Pacific. The Philippines, which is chairing the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) this year, is hosting both summits.According to the ministry of external affairs (MEA), Prime Minister will attend a dinner hosted by Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr on November 16 before participating in the India-Asean Summit and the East Asia Summit process on November 17.Bilateral meetings with other leaders are also being planned.Speaking at a special briefing, MEA secretary (East) Rudrendra Tandon said India's engagement with Asean, both as a regional grouping and with individual member countries, was an important part of its Act East policy."We strongly believe that as an Indian Ocean country that abuts this very important Southeast Asian maritime zone, a strong strategic relationship with the Asean member states, as a collective as well as individually, is good for both of us," Tandon said.Maritime security, regional stability in focusMaritime cooperation is expected to feature prominently in the discussions, particularly as India and Asean share adjoining maritime zones and face common regional security challenges.India and Asean marked 2026 as the Year of Maritime Cooperation, with several activities aimed at highlighting their shared maritime interests.New Delhi believes closer strategic cooperation with Southeast Asian countries will help both sides deal with changing geopolitical developments and contribute to peace and stability across Asia.The East Asia Summit, an Asean-led forum involving regional and major global powers, will provide another platform for leaders to discuss international security issues and matters of common concern.This year's summit process is being held under the theme "navigating the future", with leaders expected to focus on strengthening cooperation and building resilience amid global uncertainties.Trade ties and AITIGA reviewEconomic cooperation will also be an important part of India's engagement with Asean.Bilateral trade between India and the regional bloc stands at around $122 billion, making Asean one of India's major trading partners.India is also pushing for an early conclusion to the ongoing review of the India-Asean Trade in Goods Agreement (AITIGA), which New Delhi hopes will help address trade imbalances and improve market access.Tandon said discussions on the review were continuing, while acknowledging that negotiations involving multiple countries take time.BrahMos, South China Sea and MyanmarDefence cooperation between India and Asean countries has also gained momentum in recent years.The Philippines became India's first foreign customer for the BrahMos supersonic cruise missile in 2022, signing a $375-million deal for three shore-based anti-ship missile batteries.Philippine defence secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr recently indicated that Manila was interested in acquiring additional systems and had submitted a wish list to India.On the South China Sea, India has maintained that any Asean-China Code of Conduct should be consistent with international law, particularly the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS).The situation in Myanmar is another issue likely to feature in regional discussions. India has opposed diplomatic isolation of Myanmar, citing its geographical proximity, shared 1,643-km border and major connectivity projects, including the Kaladan Multi-Modal Transit Transport Project.Myanmar is expected to be represented in Manila by a foreign ministry official.Quad summit, possible PM Modi-Trump meetingThe Manila visit has also drawn attention amid discussions around a possible Quad leaders' summit involving India, the US, Japan and Australia.US secretary of state Marco Rubio had indicated last month that the Quad summit was planned alongside the wider meetings in the Philippines. However, the MEA said it had no confirmed information on the meeting or a possible interaction between PM Modi and US President Donald Trump.A meeting between PM Modi and Trump, if scheduled, would come amid ongoing India-US trade negotiations and following recent setbacks for the Republican Party in the US midterm elections.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.summary: US President Donald Trump is set to fly to Asia on Monday aboard the aircraft gifted by Qatar, but questions remain over whether the plane has undergone
articles.body: US President Donald Trump is set to fly to Asia on Monday aboard the aircraft gifted by Qatar, but questions remain over whether the plane has undergone the extensive security upgrades that the White House had planned for MAGA supremo, NBC News reported, citing two US officials.The aircraft's planned overhaul had drawn attention in July after a security threat from Iran forced Trump to fly back from Turkey aboard a secret military plane. The incident raised questions about the security arrangements surrounding the Qatari-gifted jet.Trump is expected to visit the Philippines to attend the Asean Summit, a key gathering of leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean), the regional bloc's highest decision-making forum.Trump had repeatedly said the aircraft would be taken out of service for major modifications so it could “go into any territory”. In September, he said the work would “take about 60 days”. However, the aircraft continued to be used for presidential travel, including a trip to Ireland that month and several journeys during Trump's October midterm campaign blitz.According to NBC News, the plane has undergone periodic maintenance and received some improvements, but it is unclear whether the larger security upgrades have been completed. One of the officials said a longer period of upgrades was still expected, although the work would not take the full 60 days.The changes made so far have reportedly focused largely on the aircraft's interior. One official described them as “cosmetic” enhancements, which did not include the more extensive work the White House had earlier said was planned.A senior administration official declined to discuss the specific modifications, telling NBC News: “We don’t comment on specific upgrades or modifications to Air Force Once. We maintain a consistent posture that ensures a safe, secure, and reliable capability for the President of the United States and routinely evolve the capability as required to maintain that posture. It is the greatest Presidential plane ever built.”Trump had first spoken about the planned overhaul in July, saying the aircraft already had considerable capabilities but would soon be sent for further modifications.“But as I understand it, in about a month ​or so, they’re gonna send it to have it be maxed out,” he said. “It’ll take about a month.”He did not explain what the proposed upgrades would involve. The White House has also not clarified why the initial estimate of around 30 days later increased to 60 days.Then-White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt had said in July that the aircraft was “perfectly safe” for domestic and overseas travel. However, she confirmed that further work was planned, saying it would “receive additional upgrades and enhancements in the fall which will take approximately one month to complete.”You use AI every day. articles.summary: Towering waves battered California's coastline over the weekend, with dramatic videos capturing massive swells crashing against piers, flooding beaches
articles.body: Towering waves battered California's coastline over the weekend, with dramatic videos capturing massive swells crashing against piers, flooding beaches and sending seawater surging onto coastal streets. The powerful surf forced the closure of several iconic piers across Northern and Southern California, while authorities warned residents and visitors to stay away from the water.The National Weather Service's Bay Area office warned that waves reaching up to 35 feet (10.6 metres) were possible, along with dangerous rip currents and sneaker waves.“Stay out of the water, stay off rocks and jetties, and never turn your back on the ocean!” the weather service said in a social media post.The danger was prominent on Saturday when waves exceeding 50 feet (15.2 metres) were recorded in San Mateo County, just south of San Francisco. Despite the hazardous conditions, surfers flocked to Mavericks Beach near Half Moon Bay to take on the giant swells.Further south, the Santa Cruz County Sheriff's Office issued an evacuation warning for areas near the coastal town of Capitola, which bore the brunt of the powerful surf.In Southern California, videos showed waves crashing against several piers, including those in Ventura, Manhattan Beach, Huntington Beach and Pacific Beach in San Diego. All were closed over the weekend amid the dangerous conditions.At La Jolla Cove near San Diego, known for its sea lion population, seawater spilled over the beach and surged up a staircase leading down to the sand.Conditions began to ease by Sunday afternoon, but forecasters warned that large waves could persist throughout the week.The powerful ocean conditions come amid an ongoing super El Niño, which has warmed ocean waters and caused seawater to expand.You use AI every day. articles.title: Estonia closes all Russia border crossings after alleged sabotage; Moscow cries 'Russophobia'
articles.summary: Estonia has announced plans to shut all its border crossing points with Russia from December 1, triggering a sharp reaction from Moscow, which has accused
articles.body: Estonia has announced plans to shut all its border crossing points with Russia from December 1, triggering a sharp reaction from Moscow, which has accused Tallinn of indulging in “aggressive and unrestrained Russophobia”. The decision comes after Estonian authorities accused Russia's military intelligence agency, the GRU, of ordering an attempted sabotage attack on a defence technology company in the country.Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova hit back at the announcement on Sunday, questioning Estonia's intentions and describing the proposed border closure as another example of hostility towards Moscow. “If these are their real plans, then they fit into yet another bout of aggressive and unrestrained Russophobia,” Zakharova told Russian state news agency TASS.What triggered Estonia's border closure decisionThe announcement followed the detention of eight people suspected of attempting to set fire to Threod Systems, a defence technology company based in Viimsi, near the capital Tallinn. According to Estonian authorities, the suspects attempted to break into the facility shortly after 3 am on Saturday with the intention of starting a fire and causing an explosion.Prosecutor General Astrid Asi said the company's security personnel managed to stop the attack before it could cause significant damage. No injuries were reported. All eight suspects are residents of neighbouring Latvia, while five have been remanded in custody.Estonia's Internal Security Service, known as KAPO, said intelligence gathered during its investigation indicated that the attempted sabotage had been commissioned by Russia's GRU military intelligence agency. Threod Systems manufactures long-range reconnaissance and attack drones.Prime Minister Kristen Michal described the incident as part of Russia's wider hybrid campaign against Europe, alleging that Moscow was seeking to weaken support for Ukraine and reduce pressure on Russia. He said closing the border would help reduce security risks, particularly as Russian intelligence agencies were believed to exploit border crossings to exert influence.Estonia currently has three operational crossing points with Russia at Narva, Luhamaa and Koidula, which allow pedestrian and freight movement. The government has not specified how long the closure will remain in force or announced a reopening date.Ukraine has welcomed Tallinn's decision, calling it an example of how European countries should respond to alleged Russian sabotage operations.Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha said Estonia had demonstrated that Russian sabotage could have consequences beyond diplomatic condemnation, adding that the approach deserved wider support across Europe.You use AI every day. articles.title: Land acquired, compensation delayed: When must govt pay interest? Himachal Pradesh HC answers
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Himachal Pradesh high court has directed the Central government and the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) to pay 7.5 percent
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Himachal Pradesh high court has directed the Central government and the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) to pay 7.5 percent annual interest to two landowners for the 367-day delay in depositing compensation for land acquired for a national highway project.The court said that they were entitled to interest because the compensation amount was not deposited for a year after the award was passed. It allowed the petition and directed the authorities to deposit the interest amount within two weeks.Why did the landowners approach the high court?As per the court order, the petitioners owned land in Sirmaur district. Their land was acquired for widening and four-laning National Highway 72’s Paonta Sahib-Ballupur bypass.The authority passed the compensation award on February 14, 2022, for the acquired land. The two petitioners were entitled to Rs 3,78,76,160, with each having a share of Rs 1,89,38,080. They had already been paid interest from March 26, 2021, to February 14, 2022.However, the government deposited the compensation amount with the sub-divisional officer, who was the competent authority for land acquisition, on February 16, 2023, 367 days after the award. Even after the deposit, the amount was withheld following instructions from the government not to release it until arbitration proceedings challenging the award were concluded. The arbitration was eventually decided against the government.The petitioners approached the high court seeking interest at 18 percent per annum from the date of the award until actual payment. During the proceedings, the amount was disbursed through a communication dated July 24, 2024, leaving the court to decide only the dispute over interest.The authorities opposed the demand, arguing that the award had been challenged in arbitration and that the landowners had delayed handing over possession, affecting highway construction. They also reserved the right to recover the increased construction cost from the petitioners, a claim the court did not decide.Why did the high court direct payment of interest?Justice Sandeep Sharma noted that the compensation amount was deposited on February 16, 2023, while the arbitrator stayed the award only on July 23, 2024. There was no stay during the 367-day period for which the petitioners claimed interest.The court rejected the argument that the landowners had delayed handing over the land. It said that under Section 3D(2) of the National Highways Act, 1956, the land becomes the property of the Central government once the acquisition declaration is published.“With the issuance of Notification, as detailed herein above, land came to be vested absolutely in Central Government, in terms of S.3D. If it is so, ground otherwise attempted to be raised by Mr. R.K. Khidtta that on account of delay in handing over possession of land, construction of National Highway was delayed, is of no consequence/relevance, especially for considering the relief prayed for in the instant proceedings,” the court noted.The court also rejected the authorities’ argument that compensation could be withheld because of pending arbitration proceedings.“Since there was a delay in deposit of award amount for one year and during afore period, no stay order by any competent court of law was passed, petitioners ought to have been released amount of compensation alongwith interest for the period with effect from 15.2.2022 to 16.2.2023,” it added.The court examined Sections 3G and 3H of the Act, which deal with determination and deposit of compensation. It noted that the Central government was required to deposit the amount with the competent authority, which was responsible for paying it to the landowners.Allowing the petition, the high court directed the Centre and NHAI to calculate and pay 7.5 percent annual interest on the petitioners’ share for the period from February 14, 2022, to February 16, 2023, lower than the 18 percent sought. The amount must be deposited with the competent authority within two weeks, after which the petitioners can apply for its release. Failure to comply will attract interest at 18 percent per annum from the date of the order until actual payment, in addition to the 7.5 percent.

articles.title: Kevin Short found a gold ring bearing the words ‘I live in hope’ just 15 minutes into a metal-detecting search; the British Museum authenticated the centuries-old find, now heading to auction for up to £3,000
articles.summary: A metal-detecting search in a Warwickshire field led to an unexpected discovery for Kevin Short.
articles.body: A metal-detecting search in a Warwickshire field led to an unexpected discovery for Kevin Short. Just 15 minutes after beginning the search with his friends, he found a gold ring buried a few inches beneath the soil. The ring carried a short inscription that read, “I live in hope”.Short was surprised by how quickly he found something valuable. The discovery was later examined by the British Museum, which confirmed that the ring was authentic and dated it to between the 16th and 18th centuries. It is now set to go under the hammer at an auction in December, with an estimated value of £2,000 to £3,000.The discovery was particularly exciting for Short, who has been involved in metal detecting for several years. Speaking about the find, he said, “I was genuinely surprised to find something like this so quickly… I knew straight away it was gold, although I had no idea of its quality or how significant it might be.”He told the Banbury Guardian that the search had barely begun when he spotted the ring. “We’d only been searching for around 10 to 15 minutes. I saw it glinting and picked it out from the soil.”The moment became even more memorable when Short and his friends realised what they had found. “When we realised what we’d found, we did the gold dance! It’s certainly not bad for a day’s work,” he said. Short described it as his most exciting discovery after years of metal detecting.The find also came a day after Short had returned another piece of jewellery to someone who had lost it. This coincidence made the discovery of the gold ring even more meaningful for him.Ring found after an act of kindnessThe evening before discovering the gold ring, Short had found an earring while metal detecting. He posted a photograph of it in a metal-detecting group on Facebook, hoping that someone might be able to identify it.The post received an unexpected response. A person contacted him and said the earring looked exactly like one that had belonged to their late sister. The original earring had been lost, and the person believed that Short might have found its missing counterpart.Short offered to send the earring back without asking for any payment. He eventually contacted the owner through Facebook and posted it to them free of charge.The following evening, he found the gold ring in the Warwickshire field. The sequence of events made him wonder whether his earlier gesture of kindness had brought him some good fortune.The ring was discovered only a few inches below the surface. Its inscription, “I live in hope”, was one of the most distinctive features of the find. According to a caption published by the Banbury Guardian, the words appear on the band with crosses separating them. The full inscription reads: “x I x LIVE x IN x HOPE x”.What makes the gold ring a posy ring?The gold ring belongs to a category of jewellery known as posy rings. These rings are recognised for their short inscriptions, which are usually engraved on the inside of the band.According to BBC News, such inscriptions are a defining feature of posy rings. National Museums Scotland has also described them as some of the most evocative objects of love in its collections.The words engraved on Short's ring give it a distinctive character. The message, “I live in hope”, is a short expression, but its original meaning and the person for whom it was intended remain unknown.The British Museum examined the ring and confirmed its authenticity. Its assessment placed the object somewhere between the 16th and 18th centuries. This means the ring could be several hundred years old, although the exact year in which it was made has not been established.There are also unanswered questions about its history. It is not known who owned the ring, who commissioned it or how it came to be buried in the Warwickshire field. Its inscription offers a small clue about the message someone wanted to preserve, but the identity of that person remains a mystery.Auction estimate puts the ring at up to £3,000The ring will be offered for sale by Holloways Auctioneers, based in Oxfordshire, on December 2. It has been given an estimated value of between £2,000 and £3,000.Amanda Butler, director at Holloways, said the appeal of such discoveries lies partly in the questions they leave unanswered.“One of the things I love about pieces like this, is that they always carry so many unanswered questions. Who wore it? Was there a special reason for the inscription?” she said, as quoted by British Heritage magazine.She also spoke about the message engraved on the ring and its significance. “‘I Live In Hope’ is such a beautiful sentiment, particularly when you consider that it’s been carried through the generations.”Butler said the ring's history would probably never be fully known, even though it was interesting to imagine the story behind it. “There’s a whole story here that we’ll probably never know, but it’s lovely to imagine,” she said.You use AI every day. articles.summary: Daniel Noboa says US personnel in the country for ‘temporary activities’.
articles.body:
Ecuadoran President Daniel Noboa has denied that the United States has a military base in his country near the port city of Guayaquil after voters rejected a referendum to allow foreign military sites.

Noboa’s denial came on Sunday after the AFP news agency last month documented an unusual deployment of US aircraft at the Taura Air Base and the installation of dozens of tents and infrastructure work.

It also identified about 20 US military flights at the base from June to mid-October and obtained documents referring to the presence of US soldiers.

Noboa said US personnel were at the airbase solely for “temporary activities” as part of cooperation between the two countries.

“Sometimes there’s a specific mission. Sometimes there’s a specific operation,” he told the digital news outlet Altavoz. “We work together. It’s not an American base. It’s an Ecuadoran base.”

Noboa did not address the US aircraft and sidestepped the journalist’s request to visit the Taura base.

The US deployment raised questions about its legality, including among senior Ecuadoran military officials. The then-air force commander, General Mauricio Salazar, asked the armed forces to clarify the legality of the deployment, AFP said, citing a letter sent in September.

Salazar was subsequently removed from his post and reassigned to less senior duties.

The scope of the US military presence has not been disclosed, but Quito and Washington have been strengthening their cooperation in the fight against drug trafficking in the region.

The Pentagon, its Southern Command and Ecuador’s air force did not respond to requests for information when the AFP investigation was published in October.

Noboa had campaigned to change the constitution and reverse a ban on foreign military bases, but Ecuadorans voted against it in a referendum in November last year.

According to Human Rights Watch, the US has arguably become Ecuador’s main partner in its crackdown on organised criminal groups in the region and has been providing equipment, training, intelligence and direct military support.

The New York-based rights watchdog has called the partnership “perilous” as “both governments have engaged in serious human rights violations fuelled by their insistence on framing their confrontations with organised crime groups as a kind of war”.

The administration of US President Donald Trump has struck boats it has alleged were transporting illegal drugs through international waters.

During Trump’s first term, he pondered bombing drug labs in Mexico. Since retaking office in January last year, he moved to formalise his rhetoric, designating several Latin America-based cartels as “foreign terrorist organisations”.

images.caption: Ecuadoran President Daniel Noboa campaigned to change the constitution and reverse a ban on foreign military bases [File: Adriano Machado/Reuters]

articles.title: Trump-Xi-Putin meeting has ‘groundbreaking significance,’ China says
articles.summary: China’s Foreign Ministry said on Monday that this week’s trilateral meeting between the Chinese, US and Russian leaders will promote world peace and stability.
articles.body: BEIJING — China’s Foreign Ministry said Monday that this week’s trilateral meeting between the U.S., Chinese and Russian leaders is of “groundbreaking significance” and will promote world peace and stability. The meeting between President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin will take place Thursday in China’s southern city of Shenzhen, the site of this week’s APEC summit. Trump will raise efforts to reduce nuclear arms at the meeting, the White House said last week. China has rebuffed attempts to talk about nuclear arms with Russia and the United States, which have the largest stockpiles of such weapons. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters in Beijing this would be the first face-to-face meeting among the three heads of state. “They will exchange views in depth on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations, which is of groundbreaking significance,” she added. Under the current circumstances, the three countries bear an important responsibility to cooperate in addressing global challenges and to promote world peace and stability, Mao said. “Stronger communication among China, Russia, and the United States, along with managing differences and stabilizing relations, serves the interests of all three countries,” she added. It also meets the expectations of the international community, and helps “stabilize the global situation and advance dialogue and cooperation.” Mao did not give details of what exactly is on the agenda for the trilateral meeting. Speaking in Manila on Monday, United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said the world body is prepared to support any denuclearization effort that may arise from the summit of the three countries. China has said it was more appropriate for Russia and the U.S. to speak directly because of their large arsenals. The U.N. has long advocated nuclear disarmament, warning that rising geopolitical tension and growing rivalry among major powers have fueled global nuclear risks.

images.caption: Russian President Vladimir Putin; U.S. President Donald Trump; Chinese President Xi

articles.title: Antimicrobial resistance could kill 39 million people over 25 years: WHO
articles.summary: UN’s health agency says growing resistance to antibiotics and other medicines threatens ‘future of modern medicine’.
articles.body:
The World Health Organization (WHO) has warned that growing antimicrobial resistance could cause 39 million deaths over the next 25 years as it threatens to make routine surgery and childbirth life-threatening.

Senior officials from the United Nations health agency said on Monday progress in prevention, diagnosis and the appropriate use of antibiotics remained too slow to meet global targets.

“Antibiotic resistance – but broadly, we are talking about antimicrobial resistance, or AMR – is widespread and threatening the future of modern medicine,” Jean-Pierre Nyemazi, acting director of the WHO’s AMR department, told a virtual conference of the 6th Annual Global Media Forum on AMR.

“Unlike COVID-19, which was very visible, drug-resistant infections have been taking people’s lives for years without us noticing it and raising the alarm as we should,” he said.

In 2021 alone, it was directly responsible for more than one million deaths and linked to about 4.7 million others, according to WHO figures.

An investigation into the progress of the fight against antimicrobial resistance in 183 countries this year revealed that nearly nine in 10 countries had a national action plan against the phenomenon. In 2017, the figure was just about four in 10.

Pravasha Prakash, an AMR technical officer with the global health agency, said only 42 countries – less than one in five – had a plan that was financed, implemented and monitored.

“Countries are moving forward in every step, but progress still needs to be speeded up to reach the 2030 targets,” she added.

The latest global surveillance data show that, in 2023, one in every six laboratory-confirmed bacterial infections flagged to the WHO was resistant to antibiotics used to treat it.

Sylvia Bertagnolo, head of surveillance for AMR at the WHO, said, “Without testing, clinicians must treat without knowing the cause of infection or which antibiotic will work.”

The WHO announced the release of two new tools designed to help countries strengthen diagnostic capabilities.

The first defines the tests that should be available at every level of the healthcare system, from primary care centres to referral hospitals.

The second compiles 73 laboratory procedures, from sample collection to the identification of pathogens and antibiotic susceptibility testing.

The agency added that infection prevention, vaccination, improved access to water and sanitation, and the appropriate use of antimicrobials are the main levers to combat the issue.

articles.title: Ukraine launches biggest drone attack on Russia since war began
articles.summary: Ukraine hit a strategically important bridge and targeted oil refineries in what Russian defense ministry data showed on Monday was the biggest overnight drone attack on Russia since the start of full-scale war in 2022.
articles.body: Ukraine hit a strategically important bridge and targeted oil refineries in what Russian defense ministry data showed on Monday was the biggest overnight drone attack on Russia since the start of full-scale war in 2022. Russia said its air defense forces had brought down 1,336 Ukrainian drones across 16 regions, surpassing the 1,254 drones that were registered as shot down on October 29. The scale and frequency of Ukrainian drone attacks has grown as Russia has increased its own drone and missile strikes in an intensifying war of attrition in which each side is attacking energy facilities and other important infrastructure. Attacks have continued despite U.S.-brokered peace talks in Abu Dhabi last week, the first in nine months, and separate meetings that two US envoys had with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said that around 600 Ukrainian drones had been launched at the Moscow region surrounding the Russian capital since Sunday evening, 191 of which had been brought down. Russia’s Defense Ministry said Ukrainian drones had also been brought down over Crimea, the Black Sea peninsula which Russia seized and annexed from Ukraine in 2014, and over the waters of the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea. The road and rail bridge that connects Crimea to the Russian region of Krasnodar, a signature infrastructure project associated with Putin, was struck overnight, said Sergei Aksyonov, the Russian-backed governor of Crimea. The Kremlin called the damage minor. Road traffic was temporarily suspended while repairs were undertaken, but rail traffic was continuing as normal, the transport ministry said. Yuri Slyusar, the governor of the Rostov region, home to various oil facilities, said in a statement that fires had broken out at four industrial sites in Azov after the Ukrainian attack. Emergency services were working at the scenes of the incidents, he said. Local officials said a fire had broken out at an unnamed industrial facility in Ilsky in the Krasnodar region and that falling drone debris has injured six people, including children. Ilsky is home to an oil refinery. Ukraine has sharply increased its strike campaign on Russian oil refineries since the end of October, launching attacks which Zelenskyy said late on Sunday had knocked out over half of Russia’s refining capacity, something Reuters was not able to independently verify immediately. Two industry sources told Reuters last week that the renewed Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian oil refineries had reduced Russia’s oil refining capacity by about 30%. Russian officials and media said last week that, as a result, fuel shortages had returned to at least half a dozen Russian regions, but that so far there was no repeat of scenes seen over the summer when some motorists were forced to queue for hours at filling stations. Kyiv and Moscow agreed on a major exchange of prisoners during last week’s talks but there was no significant breakthrough on other key issues including territory. Russia holds about a fifth of Ukrainian land but the front line in the war has remained largely static for months.

images.caption: The symbolic bridge inaugurated by Russia's President Vladimir Putin in 2018, is logistically crucial for Moscow.

articles.title: Nvidia scandals throw wrench into Trump’s meeting with Xi Jinping
articles.summary: The evolving espionage and extramarital affair drama surrounding Nvidia and its fallen founder, Jensen Huang, is threatening to cast a dark cloud over President Trump’s expected meeting this week with Chinese premier Xi Jinping. Trump is traveling to the Philippines and China this week for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations Summit (ASEAN) and the…
articles.body:
The evolving espionage and extramarital affair drama surrounding Nvidia and its fallen founder, Jensen Huang, is threatening to cast a dark cloud over President Trump’s expected meeting this week with Chinese premier Xi Jinping.

Trump is traveling to the Philippines and China this week for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations Summit (ASEAN) and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC), respectively, where artificial intelligence, trade and security issues are sure to be top agenda items.

The president is heading to Asia at one of his weakest points politically following a clobbering in the midterm elections. He’s also lost one of his closest allies in the technology world after Jensen Huang resigned this week over a series of extramarital affairs — including one with potential national security implications.

Nvidia founder Jensen Huang had an affair with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese spy. U.S. officials concluded that she was passing information to Beijing, but China has denied that she is a spy.

Craig Singleton, a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, said he doubts Trump will bring up the Jensen Huang scandal with Xi.

“Trump has stood by Huang personally, and my read is that he sees espionage as something major powers just do to each other,” Singleton said on a preview call with reporters. “He wants a very successful meeting and to show that he can manage the relationship with Xi Jinping.”

Trump said last week he wouldn’t bring up the Jensen Huang situation when meeting with Xi, but that he’s “sure President Xi will ask me about it.”

Jensen Huang previously accompanied Trump to Beijing during his May trip. Trump initially suggested he might invite the former tech firm CEO on this week’s trip, but since then plans have changed.

Beyond Jensen Huang’s affairs, the Trump administration is also facing growing questions over why Megaspeed was not blacklisted due to suspicions it was helping China evade chip export controls. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Friday morning pinned the blame on the Commerce Department during an appearance on CNBC’s “Squawk Box.”

APEC is being hosted this year in Shenzhen from Nov. 18-19.

Trump met with Xi twice this year, in Beijing in May and in Washington in September. While trade was the center of the talks in Beijing, AI was a bigger focus in Washington and will surely be brought up in Shenzhen.

Trump has consistently said that the U.S. needs to win the AI race against China, but Xi in September signaled that the U.S. and China have a responsibility to make sure AI remains human-controlled “and serves the well-being of the people.”

Kyle Chan, a fellow at the John L. Thornton China Center at Brookings, wrote that “expectations for U.S.-China discussions about AI should remain low.”

“Many worry that the United States and China will move too slowly in the face of growing AI risks and rapid improvements in capabilities,” Chan wrote . “But equally worrying is the risk that official U.S.-China AI talks might get derailed at the outset as mounting expectations collide with deep mutual distrust between the two countries.”

Elon Musk is expected to go on the trip but is not expected to attend the trilateral meeting.

Edgard Kagan, an expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, said the Nvidia drama would only make progress harder.

“I think that it doesn’t sound like we have made a huge amount of headway on AI. And my guess is that what’s happened with Jensen Huang probably means that it’s even more difficult to make headway right now,” he said.

There’s a “vast gap” and lack of trust between the U.S. and China on this issue, he said.

“The problem for the Chinese is if they sign something, if they accept anything jointly with the U.S., it runs the risk of appearing that they have accepted sort of institutionalizing that gap,” he said.

The U.S. and China also have much to talk about on trade. The two countries have extended their bilateral trade truce through Jan. 10. The deal, first struck in October, lowered U.S. tariffs on Chinese exports and saw China agree to suspend its export controls on rare metals.

Experts are cautioning against expecting any major breakthroughs. Trump and Xi’s meeting is expected to be brief, happening on the sidelines of APEC, with another meeting taking place in December at the Group of 20 gathering in Florida.

“I see Shenzhen as a long layover on the way to Miami,” Singleton said. “By December, all the election dust will have settled. Both leaders and their trade teams are expected in Miami, and they’ll be down to the wire to do something about the trade truce, which expires in early January.”

Extending the trade truce will likely lay the groundwork for further meetings in 2027, said one former U.S. official, who asked to remain anonymous because of the sensitivity around the meetings.

The truce allows the U.S. to avoid triggering China to further strangle America’s access to its critical minerals supply. Beijing is keen to avoid retaliatory actions from the U.S. on further denying China’s access to U.S. technology.

Congress is pushing hard for increased scrutiny on export restrictions following the Jensen Huang scandal and concerns that Alice Huang’s Megaspeed funneled Nvidia’s chips to China.

Trump is expected to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Xi for trilateral talks on the sidelines of APEC, the White House confirmed Friday.

The discussions will include denuclearization and Iran, U.S. officials said.

“I would characterize this as the entry point, the first conversation, certainly at the leader level, between these countries,” a senior U.S. official told reporters, adding that it’s “hopefully a conversation that can be productive going forward.”

China has rebuffed any efforts to constrain its ability to build up its nuclear weapons arsenal. Both countries have assisted Iran in hitting back against the U.S. and its partners in the Middle East over nine months of war.

Jonathan Czin, a fellow in the China Center with the Brookings Institution, expressed pessimism about that path in a briefing.

“It is difficult to envisage a scenario in which a meeting among Trump, Xi, and Putin has a happy outcome for the United States and its interests,” Czin wrote.

The proposed meeting has been compared to Yalta, when the U.S., United Kingdom and Russia met after World War II to divide up global spheres of influence.

“For Trump, I think the appeal is that he gets to put himself at the center of a meeting with two leaders he believes he can deal with personally,” Singleton said of the potential trilateral meeting.

Notably, the senior U.S. official said that the president does not intend to discuss Ukraine.

Another important point on Trump’s agenda is the fate of two Americans jailed in China.

Youlin Chen, a seismologist, has been held for more than two years (he was detained on Nov. 5, 2024) while academic Min Zin was arrested in June. The State Department has labeled both men as “wrongfully detained.” China rejects this label.

The Trump administration has freed 115 Americans unjustly detained abroad, according to a count by the State Department.

But China has failed to engage on either case, even as Trump has raised them multiple times.

“I hope President Trump will demand Min Zin’s immediate and unconditional release when he sees President Xi at the APEC Summit next week,” Sylvia Zin, Min Zin’s wife, said in a statement to The Hill.

“I am grateful for everything the Administration has done up until this point, and hope that they will successfully secure his release so he can spend the holidays at home with our family.”

ASEAN is being hosted this year in Manila, and Trump is expected to make a stop there on Nov. 17 before heading to APEC. He is scheduled to meet with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., along with other leaders. The discussions are expected to focus on regional security, strategic cooperation, economic growth and digital transformation.

Trump will also sign a trade deal with Thailand, White House spokesperson Olivia Wales told reporters Friday.

Singleton said he’s hearing that the Filipinos want Trump to leave the summit with the “impression of the Philippines as a model ally.”

“The real meeting to watch is Trump and Marcos — like a clear public reaffirmation of the U.S. commitment to the Philippines in the South China Sea, I think would send a signal that Beijing will hear before Trump ever lands in Shenzhen,” he said.

Trump will also participate in a Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (Quad) meeting with Australia, India and Japan, where peace, prosperity and security in the Indo-Pacific region will be discussed, Wales said. It will be the first leader-level Quad meeting of this administration.

“I think it’s always much better for the United States if the president engages with key allies and partners before seeing the Chinese,” Kagan said. “Because it’s a reminder to them that we do have a network, and that our real power isn’t just what we’re able to do ourselves, but the fact that we have this network of allies and partners and countries that want good relations with us in the region and around the world.”

The visit will end with “commercial deals and strategic investments that strengthen American security and prosperity,” the White House said.

images.caption: President Trump listens as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang speaks during an event about investing in America in the Cross Hall of the White House, April 30, 2025, in Washington.

articles.title: They wanted to spend forever on a cruise. Then everything fell apart
articles.summary: Villa Vie  cruise ship Odyssey promised its residents the dream of traveling the globe indefinitely. But then the dream sank and former passengers are reeling from the consequences.
articles.body: When Kit Cassingham boarded the Odyssey residential cruise ship, she saw it as her new home — traveling the globe, with no end in sight. She had just one reservation: “The poor Odyssey … I always thought that was an unfortunate name,” Cassingham told CNN Travel, recalling the epic Greek poem about a dramatic maritime journey. “I was slightly aware of what the original ‘Odyssey’ adventure was like, and I thought, ‘I don’t like the sense of that. That’s not quite the adventure I want to be on.’ But in some ways, that’s exactly the adventure we’ve been on…” Cassingham and her husband Randy didn’t spend the last two years fighting cyclops or dodging sea sirens. But there were times when it felt like the ocean god, Poseidon, had cursed the vessel they called home. Villa Vie’s Odyssey was not an ordinary cruise ship. As a “residential” vessel, passengers could purchase cabins and live aboard full-time as it circumnavigated the globe. Residents like Cassingham sold their houses and downsized their belongings, viewing the Odyssey as a permanent home. The ship, operated by a residential cruise startup called Villa Vie, got off to a rocky start when it got stuck in Belfast, Northern Ireland for four months at the beginning of its voyage, due to reported issues with repairs and certifications. The 642-foot, eight-deck Odyssey was a refurbished 33-year-old ship. “And then it’s been two years of missed ports and cash calls and all kinds of problems,” said Cassingham. “But we developed a wonderful community. We saw and experienced wonderful things.” Despite the ups and downs, Cassingham loved life at sea. “That was our home,” said Cassingham of her cabin. “We decorated it with our things, which are still on the ship…” While Cassingham’s belongings remain on the Odyssey, she does not. On October 26, the roughly 200 guests on board the ship were abruptly told to disembark in the port city of Sihanoukville, Cambodia. Villa Vie said it was suspending operations, releasing a statement citing “extraordinary increases in fuel costs.” The dream was over. For Cassingham, the end both came out of nowhere and didn’t. She said there had been several requests from the company for passengers to stump up more cash in recent months (and, when she thought about it, “from almost the very beginning, disguised in various ways”) and constant discussions about fuel shortages. Part of her thought the “writing was on the wall.” But Villa Vie was still advertising cabins for purchase, and Cassingham figured the owners wouldn’t be trying to sell rooms if they were on the verge of bankruptcy. In July 2026, Villa Vie had announced plans to launch a second residential cruise ship Villa Vie co-owner and executive chairman Mikael Petterson told CNN Travel that “the suspension of operations had serious consequences for residents, crew and employees.” Petterson added he understood “why residents are angry and disappointed. I don’t want to minimize their experiences or suggest every decision was handled well.” According to Petterson, Villa Vie was hopeful a potential investor and operating partner might pull through in October and save the company. That’s why he said cabins were still available for purchase at that time. He said the potential investor and operating partner signed a letter of intent for a proposed $15 million investment. “The group visited the ship in October, met with residents and answered their questions,” said Petterson. “We continued advertising cabins while the proposed transaction was under discussion. The deal did not close, and discussions abruptly ended on October 22. That changed the company’s position considerably, and we suspended cabin sales at that point.” To resident Cassingham, the end felt “pretty cold and heartless.” “The message to ‘abandon ship’ was posted on ‘Circle’, the ship/community message platform, at about 7 a.m.,” she said. “We were told we had to be off by 2 p.m. on the same day.” There was chaos as people attempted to pack. Others left everything. “People were in all kinds of moods,” said Cassingham. “Some people were furious … This woman I’m thinking of, she’s mid-80s, had spent most of her money joining, so she was crushed, devastated. There was shock. We knew it was coming. We just didn’t expect it that harshly.” ‘We loved the lifestyle’ Cassingham and her husband lived in Southwest Colorado before they were wooed by the permanent cruise concept. She’s a life coach in her early 70s and he’s a writer and publisher in his late 60s. They could both work remotely. When they discovered Villa Vie, they said they’d already lost $10,000 on another residential cruise ship venture that didn’t come to fruition. Undeterred, in 2024 the Cassinghams put their savings towards a berth on the Odyssey, purchasing a cabin for around $370,000. “That price was to give us the cabin for the life of the ship (15 years) and then move our residence to the next comparable ship,” explained Cassingham. The couple wanted to live at sea, and they believed in the dream of a residential cruise ship on a never-ending, incredible voyage. Living on the Odyssey didn’t come cheap. Earlier this year, Villa Vie Residences told CNN that five-year cabin ownership started at $59,999 and full ownership prices started at $99,999. There were various other occupancy plans. Owners also paid monthly fees — which in 2025 worked out as $2,000 per person per month for double occupancy, and $3,000 for single occupancy, according to Villa Vie. These prices were more accessible than The World, the only residential cruise ship experience currently at sea, which caters to a more upscale market with current one-bedroom cabin ownership starting price of $3.4 million. There are other residential ship projects in the works — such as the NJORD, a self-described “exclusive community at sea” — but they’ve yet to be realized. Other concepts, such as Life at Sea — which Petterson and Villa Vie CEO Kathy Villalba were initially involved in — never materialized, leaving prospective passengers high and dry. Villa Vie advertised that food and soft drinks were included in Odyssey residents’ monthly fees. So was alcohol at dinner, Wi-Fi and medical visits (but not procedures and medicines). They also spoke of round-the-clock room service, weekly housekeeping, and biweekly laundry service at no extra cost. Cassingham said some of these offerings “varied through the months of sailing.” For example, unlimited wine and beer were initially included at meals, but “some six-ish months ago, they restricted that to two glasses per meal.” She said that room service went from round-the-clock to limited hours. Petterson said there were “changes to onboard services” during the Odyssey’s two-year voyage. “Room service was never unlimited; it was a paid service. We reduced its hours because of demand and staffing challenges,” he said. “The complimentary beer and wine service at lunch and dinner was limited to two servings after we identified abuse of the policy.” For many Odyssey residents, these perks were secondary to the friendships they were forming at sea and the adventures they were having in port. “We loved the lifestyle, we loved the people, we liked seeing parts of the world we didn’t even know existed, much less thought we’d ever get there,” said Cassingham. Some parts of the world remained off limits. The Odyssey was plagued by port cancellations from the outset. Speaking to CNN earlier in 2026, Petterson blamed these on weather, as well as red tape and logistical problems in destinations where smaller tender vessels are needed to carry passengers ashore. The fallout from the Iran war and the soaring fuel prices seemingly compounded pre-existing issues. “We’ve had to remain flexible and occasionally adjust routes or port calls based on global events,” Petterson told CNN earlier this year. He said at the time that the company was attempting to create more flexible itineraries to better accommodate unpredictable events. The Odyssey started spending more time in ports and less time on the water. In an October 27 press release announcing the company was suspending operations, Villa Vie said that monthly fuel expenses in parts of Asia which had historically averaged approximately $1,800 per month per-cabin, had recently reached an estimated $6,000 to $8,000. Strapped for cash As fuel costs ballooned, residents told CNN that they were called upon for extra cash and loans throughout the voyage. Cassingham said they were often asked to sign non-disclosure agreements about these cash calls. Petterson said: “Passengers were not asked to sign NDAs simply because they were residents. An NDA was required only if someone chose to invest in the company’s equity and receive confidential, nonpublic financial information.” Petterson said Villa Vie was “always 100% capitalized by its residents, who owned almost 90% of the company.” The company had no outside source of funding, according to Petterson. “Residents who were also shareholders could be asked to participate in funding the company, but those requests were voluntary,” he said. Petterson said that in April 2026, the company “offered residents the opportunity to participate in a fuel loan and introduced a voluntary fuel surcharge.” Cassingham and her husband briefly disembarked the ship in August in Singapore because Randy, who has cancer, was undergoing a planned medical procedure. “As we left, we heard, ‘We don’t have enough fuel nor the money to buy it. What are we going to do?’” recalled Cassingham. “The residents pulled enough money together to buy the fuel to last, it was supposed to last a month or so … Of course, it didn’t last as long as they said it would.” Cassingham briefly wondered if she’d ever get back on the ship, or if everything would fall apart while they were away. In the end they did return, but in Hong Kong, there was another emergency cash call. Then, in Thailand in September, there was talk of new investors swooping in to save the ship. “We were real close to the investors working out a deal to buy it,” said Cassingham, Instead, the ship sailed to Cambodia. According to Petterson, at that stage, Villa Vie believed the voyage was in a position to continue. “When we left Thailand, we had a $15 million investment coming in and had no reason to doubt that the transaction would come through,” said Petterson. Instead, the voyage came to an end. The Cambodian city known for its Chinese-run casinos seemed an “inopportune port” in which to be abandoned, said Cassingham. The Odyssey relied on Starlink internet and there was no connection in Sihanoukville. No Wi-Fi, combined with poor phone coverage “made planning difficult.” The border to Thailand was closed and the nearest international airport was some three hours away. “All that said, the Cambodians were very gracious, warm, and supportive in helping us navigate our challenges,” said Cassingham. Residents scrambled to find hotels and temporary accommodation. Although passengers were allowed back on board to continue packing until the vessel left Cambodia, Cassingham said cataloguing two years of life was overwhelming — especially when most didn’t know where they were going next. “How do you gather all of your things from your life and home even in a few days and have it make sense?” she asked. Many had to leave possessions behind, with Villa Vie assuring them that anything left in their cabins would be kept safe for future retrieval. Villa Vie said via its October 27 press release that the company was “working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and identify temporary living arrangements.” Cassingham said she was sent a list of hotels — but 36 hours after disembarkation, and with no offer from Villa Vie to contribute to costs. Petterson told CNN Villa Vie did not offer accommodation and was in no position to offer financial assistance. Watching from afar The Odyssey departed Cambodia last week, and arrived in Singapore, where it was placed under arrest by authorities. The Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore said that the crew on board were “reported to be well, and arrangements for their welfare and wellbeing are being managed by the vessel’s creditors. There are no passengers on board.” A creditor ship arrest involves a vessel being held in port to secure payment for an unpaid debt or claim. Petterson told CNN that the ship has been detained by a fuel supplier, and there is “no dispute” that Villa Vie owed a debt to the fuel supplier. Watching from afar, former Odyssey resident Sharon Lane felt a melee of emotions: shock, sadness, anger, concern, relief. Lane spoke to CNN Travel about her decision to board the Odyssey in 2025 and again earlier this year as she celebrated a year on the ship. Lane also previously signed up to the failed Life at Sea venture. She wasn’t concerned, she said, by the overlap in the organizers of both projects. “I trusted them because the first time I didn’t lose any money, and I thought that meant that they had integrity, and they probably do,” Lane said in a new interview. “I think the problem is that they didn’t know what they were doing.” Lane wanted to live on the Odyssey indefinitely. She trusted the concept and trusted Villa Vie. But in the end, she left the ship this summer, “two months before it went belly up,” as she put it. Lane’s wavering started with a bout of food poisoning, which highlighted some personal underlying health conditions and led her to question the seafaring lifestyle. What cemented Lane’s decision to move on was a particular call for cash from Villa Vie in July. “They sent a demand letter to everybody that was very poorly handled, very poorly worded,” she said. “I was ill, and so the stress made me even more ill.” There were subsequent heated meetings between residents to discuss next steps, according to Lane. “The meetings were not pleasant at all,” said Lane. “A couple of the meetings I had to get up and leave, and that’s not me.” The money discussions worried Lane. If the money was needed for fuel, short term loans didn’t seem like a viable solution. “For fuel, they’re going to need it next month, and the month after that, and the month after that,” she recalled thinking. She started reflecting on some of the things that Villa Vie had spent money on, which she deemed profligate: including a “floating beach club” described by Lane as “a raft-like thing with a cabana on it and a hole in the middle which was like a swimming pool, and lounge chairs.” It took four hours for the crew to set up, she said. “Then, when people tried to walk across it, it was moving — because it’s in the open ocean and it’s moving up and down with the sea — and people were falling down,” Lane recalled. “It took two or three people to hold someone as they were walking across it.” Lane felt this toy didn’t seem especially suitable — or appealing — for the Odyssey’s older-skewing residents. “I thought, ‘This is a boy toy. Why are they buying boy toys? Don’t they know who’s on the ship?’ Evidently not. So, they spent money on that. They spent money on other things that were foolish, and then they didn’t have money for what they needed.” Petterson describes this raft as “a relatively modest amenity intended for tropical destinations, including places such as the Maldives.” The company advertised the raft — a partnership with inflatable platform company Aquabanas — in a press release in July 2025. “They were used less than we had hoped,” said Petterson. “But were intended to give residents another way to relax on anchorage days.” As Lane worried about the future of the Odyssey, she said she started to lose weight from the stress. “Then there was a meeting that was arguing back and forth with the owners and the residents, and it got pretty ugly,” she recalled. For Lane, this August showdown was the final straw. “I said, ‘I’m off the ship. I’m not in a physical state to handle it. I’m too sick. I just can’t do it.’” It took Lane a month to sort her belongings and travel arrangements. She considered moving to Portugal, but she felt the safety and familiarity of her home state of California was necessary, given her ongoing health issues. She returned at the end of August to try to rebuild her life. From her new California condo, Lane watched Villa Vie fall apart and the dream of the Odyssey sink. She missed the ship but mostly mourned the community on board. She was relieved she’d left early, but worried about those left on board. She told herself the community would come together and support each other. Cassingham also keeps coming back to the residents’ camaraderie. Many residents, including Cassingham, are still in Cambodia and she said former Odyssey passengers are making the most of this unexpected stopover. “Wherever there’s a cluster of residents, they are partying, they’re playing cards, they’re going to book clubs and plays. They’re not letting this slow them down very much, and they’re using the community to help lift their spirits, which I think is brilliant,” she said. Journey’s end The former Odyssey residents are still processing the journey’s end, and the gap between their expectations and reality. Lane said she doesn’t regret speaking to CNN about how much she loved life on the Odyssey before it all fell apart. She frequently met people who’d joined the ship because they’d read about her experiences. “I don’t have a problem with having done that,” said Lane. “Those people were mishandled by sales and the owners.” She describes one encounter with a couple who’d come to look at cabins after reading about Lane. “I said, “So, how do you like it?” They said, “Well, there’s no refrigerator in our room, and the thermostat doesn’t work.”” Lane was shocked. She had a few issues in her room, but she figured part of the reason these hadn’t been fixed was because Villa Vie were prioritizing perfecting new rooms for prospective passengers. She questioned where funds were going and if the owners would be able to keep the Odyssey afloat long term. “I can’t verify the cabin conditions described without specific details,” said Petterson. “An onboard team was responsible for preparing cabins for new residents. If a cabin was provided without a refrigerator or with a thermostat that didn’t work, that points to a failure in preparation or communication, and I’m sorry the resident encountered it.” Lane and Cassingham both express gratitude that they were able to enjoy the Odyssey and their round-the-world voyage for as long as they did. “One guy, after paying $260,000, only got to spend two weeks on the ship,” said Cassingham. “One person spent two days. It’s obscene how much people spent for such short times.” Cassingham said as far as she is aware, residents did not get any money back. “I’ve heard several people suggest class action suits, and various other reasons to sue. To the best of my knowledge, nothing has happened with that though,” she added. When asked if passengers could get refunds or reimbursements, Petterson said, “if the ship sells for enough there is potentially a claim, but I still hope for a successful restructure.” Petterson said there might be a Chapter 11 restructure — which would allow the company to reorganize debts and continue operations, instead of ceasing completely. Both Cassingham and Lane acknowledge they’re lucky to have the means to start over. Lane said she’s conscious that for many passengers who are independently wealthy, the Odyssey falling apart is “unpleasant, but not life-altering.” She’s worried about the people who sold everything to commit to the Odyssey dream. “A couple of my friends, they didn’t have much income, and they sold everything, so I’m worried about them,” Lane said. “These are not people with giant portfolios. They’re not people with pensions. They’re people who are stuck … Those are the people who get hurt.” Cassingham has accepted she may not be reunited with the belongings she and her husband left on board. “When a company is as in debt as this one is, I don’t expect a penny back,” she said. “We have decided to willingly let go … Some family heirlooms of my husband, some things that represent my character, help me remember who I want to be, who I am, where I’ve been.” There is talk of some passengers clubbing together to buy the ship. One wealthy resident reportedly has a plan for if the ship goes up for auction, as is rumored to be in the cards. “The ship will be organized for a sale if a restructure can’t be organized in time,” said Petterson. “There’s a lot of enthusiasm for it,” said Cassingham of the potential rescue missions. “I don’t know yet if Randy and I can share that enthusiasm.” Petterson said he backs residents’ efforts to purchase the Odyssey. “I support residents who are trying to raise capital and acquire the ship if it goes to auction, and I will assist in every way I can,” he said. “Any successful acquisition would require the resident group to provide the equity and fund the costs of operating the company, using an approach similar to the one used in the past. There is no guarantee an acquisition will happen, but I hope they can develop a viable plan.” Cassingham and her husband aren’t actively involved in these attempts to buy the ship. Instead, they plan to return to the US this week. But they’re not put off from cruising, and hope to embark on a river cruise before too long. They said they are also not ruling out a future residential cruise, if the right venture comes around. “We’d have to look at the business plan if we did this kind of cruise, a residential cruise again,” Cassingham said. “Make sure that the business plan is solid.” They are also planning a future return trip to Cambodia, as the country won them over. “We’re bringing people with us to experience the same warm hospitality we’ve had these three weeks,” said Cassingham. As she looks ahead to the future, Cassingham said she’s also trying to focus on the fond memories, of which she said there are so many. Even being stuck in Belfast for four months unexpectedly was “exciting,” Cassingham said. Other highlights include climbing the Rock of Gibraltar, marveling at the Chilean fjords and whitewater rafting in Australia. On board the ship, residents put on plays and Cassingham started a club called Speakers’ Corner, “to let the residents, or the crew, or guests briefly share something they know and love, and just talk about it.” Cassingham said she’s leaving the Odyssey with the desire to continue to “live life big” and “take a chance.” “You only go around once,” she said. “And if I hadn’t had these two experiences, I would be that much poorer … It was worth the chance. Yeah, we paid a little more for it, but don’t be afraid of life. Look at it, face it, and go for the gusto.” As for Lane, she’s still processing her emotions. “I’m glad I went,” she said. “I wish it hadn’t been the way it was. I wish the people that organized it were better organized. I wish they had better communication skills. I wish they had done their due diligence better on the ship. It could have been even better than it was, and it could have continued … All of that bothers me. All of that makes me angry.” But whenever she feels overwhelmed by frustration, Lane tries to focus on the incredible Odyssey community and experience. “We had a lovely time together. Made really good friends. Lots of people were really, really interested in seeing the places, and they loved seeing the places that they saw, and having experiences they did. People went bungee jumping. People went to zoos. They did all sorts of things,” she said. “I read a zillion books and made some good friends and loved the ocean and the feel of the ocean under me. In fact, I still feel the ocean under me … I’m working to get my land legs back.”

articles.title: As homes seized, Jericho’s Palestinian residents fear settler takeover
articles.summary: Palestinians are assaulted and their homes are levelled in pogrom in occupied West Bank.
articles.body:
Jericho, occupied West Bank – On November 4, Israeli settlers seized eight Palestinian homes in Jericho after a months-long secretive operation spearheaded by the internationally sanctioned Nachala settler movement and with the support of the settlement council in the northern West Bank.

As soon as we arrived at the area, known as Diyouk al-Tahta, we encountered Mustafa. Israeli settlers had barred him from his land, beating him and his elderly father, who had to be treated in hospital. His uncle and cousins faced the same abuse, and other Bedouin families who live in the area were also assaulted and forced to leave their homes in the pogrom . Many of their houses were later razed by residents of Israeli settlements, which are illegal under international law.

While we were talking to Mustafa, a settler’s car sped past, and we had to quickly move out of its way. When the dust settled, a settler had left the car and appeared to be cornering a child. He slapped the boy before he managed to get away on his bike.

I asked him what happened. The child’s eyes were red. He was struggling to hold back tears. “The settler slapped me. He was speaking in Hebrew. I didn’t understand anything. I didn’t even see him coming!” I asked the child about his name, but he sped away. Perhaps it was fear or embarrassment, or both.

Many of the homes taken over by settlers in the area were under Israeli demolition orders.

A government decision this year allowing settlers to buy Palestinian property inside Palestinian-controlled areas laid the groundwork for Israeli settlement outposts to pop up in the middle of cities, which in turn would bring the Israeli army and movement restrictions to the streets of cities like Jericho.

This is what makes the precedent set in Jenin different from other settler takeovers. In occupied East Jerusalem and the Old City of Hebron, where the army maintains direct control, settlers have taken over homes by alleging they bought the properties or claiming historical Jewish ownership predating the establishment of Israel.

Palestinian owners take their battles to Israeli courts and often prove that the documents presented by settler organisations are forged. But they rarely, if ever, succeed in keeping their homes. While Jericho is run entirely by the Palestinian Authority, the Israeli settler presence here is upending people’s lives and is in effect reversing Palestinian control.

The Palestinian Authority has launched an investigation into the takeovers, trying to ascertain if anyone facilitated them via sales to settlers, and several arrests have been made. According to the law, Palestinians may not sell their homes in the West Bank to Israelis.

Legal experts told Al Jazeera that even if money changed hands in these cases, the sales would be illegal under Palestinian and international law. These are not real estate deals. They are part of a takeover campaign.

“It’s a campaign to uproot us just as they did with others in al-Mughayyir and Turmus Aya and other villages across the West Bank,” Mahmoud Abu Fkheida told me. The Jericho farmer inherited this land from his father, who inherited it from his. Working this land is their life.

“When I leave my home to tend to my farm for an hour, I stay worried. I’m now afraid when my phone rings. I keep wondering if it’s news of them burning or attacking my home,” Mahmoud told me.

As we were filming, Israeli settlers, some of them covering their faces with cloth hoods, ambushed us. They told us that our presence is a provocation and demanded we leave.

The settlers are armed, and they have Israeli army protection. We could not challenge their orders or argue with them, so we walked away towards the homes still inhabited by their Palestinian owners.

Jericho is a city that depends on tourism. Today, the cable cars leading to the Mount of Temptation run empty while the city’s facilities below waste away. Fear is ever present, as are the settlements and outposts that surround Jericho.

On the eastern edge of the city, a new settlement towers over the rubble of Palestinian villas while the fields lie barren.

We met Abdel Qader Abu Khashan, who has been overtaken by a sense of loss and dread. “Look around you. All these homes are now under threat,” he said.

Abdel Qader says what is happening in Jericho foretells a dead-end future for Palestinians.

“It’s not fear that I feel. It’s about hope and the future. I don’t want to say they’re disappearing, but they’re becoming distant,” he said.

Back at Diyouk al-Tahta, the scene was paradoxical. Children looked unbothered by the choking reality of life in Jericho. The arid hills are behind them, and the settlers are all around them, yet they play under their mothers’ watchful eyes in the small space that remains around their homes, unaware they will grow up in the shadow of this reality and bear the scars of its consequences.
