articles.title: Women's criminal records wiped for abortion offences
articles.summary: Women arrested or convicted for having illegal abortions will have their criminal records wiped as new atomatic pardons come into force in England and Wales.
articles.body:
Women arrested or convicted for having illegal abortions will have their criminal records wiped as new automatic pardons come into force in England and Wales .

Ending the Victorian-era law should avoid traumatic experiences such as that of Nicola Packer, who was recently cleared by a jury after taking medication at home during a Covid lockdown. She had ended a pregnancy without realising she was around 26 weeks pregnant, far beyond the legal 10 week limit.

Her friend Helle Tumbridge told the BBC's Today Programme she had been "treated appallingly" until justice was served.

Labour MP Tonia Antoniazzi, who brought forward the decriminalisation amendment last year, says the change will clear the names of more than 100 women who have been "unnecessarily harmed" by an "outdated" law.

Ms Packer, who was 41 at the time, took pills called mifepristone and misoprostol, which were prescribed over the phone due to Covid restrictions, to end a pregnancy in 2020.

Prosecutors alleged that she knew she had been pregnant for more than 10 weeks, which she denied.

Jurors deliberated for more than six hours to reach their unanimous verdict, clearing her name.

Speaking with the BBC and Nicola's consent, her friend Ms Tumbridge said the whole incident was "incredibly traumatic".

"Nicky had what's known as a cryptic pregnancy - that's when you don't have any sign of a pregnancy, no baby bump, no other symptoms.

"She thought she was just a few weeks pregnant and she sought an abortion and was prescribed that by the NHS. Unfortunately, she was a lot more far gone."

Nicola experienced a stillbirth and went to hospital. The staff there called the police.

"She was arrested. She spent a time in her hospital room recovering with two police officers present, one was a man. She was treated appallingly. She was made to use the toilet with the door open in front of the police officers."

It took five years of investigations for a trial to eventually find her not guilty.

"Of course, by that point the damage had been done," says Tumbridge, "and she'll live with that trauma for the rest of her life."

At the time, The Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists said Nicola's trial demonstrated "just how outdated and harmful" that law was.

It is now no longer a criminal offence for a pregnant woman to terminate her own pregnancy at any stage.

Women affected do not need to take any action.

Minister for Victims and Tackling Violence Against Women and Girls, Alex Davies-Jones, said pardoning women for abortion offences related to their own pregnancy had been a priority.

"I'm pleased to be able to commence the change that Parliament voted for.

"For those affected, I know that clear and accessible information about what happens next is vital. Women do not have to take any direct action themselves, but can find out more information online and contact our dedicated casework team."

Heidi Stewart, from the abortion care provider BPAS, said: "While no pardon can undo the distress and trauma these women have experienced, this historic change in the law recognises the profound harm caused by their criminalisation and represents a meaningful step towards justice."

Abortion in England and Wales is legal with an authorised provider up to 24 weeks, with very limited circumstances allowing one after this time, such as when the mother's life is at risk or the child would be born with a severe disability.

It is also legal to take prescribed medication at home if a woman is less than 10 weeks pregnant.

articles.title: Gérard Depardieu drops appeal and accepts sexual assault conviction
articles.summary: French actor Gérard Depardieu said Monday he was dropping his appeal against a conviction for sexually assaulting two women on a film set and will accept the 18-month suspended sentence. He also issued an apology.
articles.body: French actor Gérard Depardieu said Monday he was dropping his appeal against a conviction for sexually assaulting two women on a film set and will accept the 18-month suspended sentence. He also issued an apology. “I was found guilty,” Depardieu said in a written statement, as his appeal trial was scheduled to open Monday in Paris. He added that he “hears it” and accepts the sentence. “I therefore offer my deep and sincere apologies to those who may have suffered,” he said. Depardieu was convicted in May 2025 of groping a 54-year-old set decorator and a 34-year-old assistant during the filming of “Les Volets Verts” (“The Green Shutters”) in 2021. He received an 18-month suspended prison sentence in a case that was widely seen as a post-#MeToo test for the country’s film industry. The court also ordered the 77-year-old Depardieu, one of the most prominent figures in French cinema for decades, to pay both accusers a total of 29,040 euros ($32,350) in fines, and that his name be listed in the national sex offender database. “On film sets, I have long hidden behind provocation and crude humor. I believed my words and some of my actions had no consequences. But they did, particularly coming from someone who held as much power as I once did,” Depardieu wrote. “I have come to understand that I belonged to a world that no longer exists,” he added. “I have therefore decided to withdraw my appeal.” The comments contrast with the actors’ statements during the trial last year, when he had strongly denied the accusations. He acknowledged using vulgar and sexual language on the film set and grabbing the set dresser’s hips during an argument, but denied that his behavior was sexual. Depardieu is expected to face other legal proceedings soon. In 2018, actor Charlotte Arnould accused him of raping her at his home. An investigating judge in August 2025 requested that the case goes to trial and a Paris appeals court is to decide next week whether it will proceed. For more than a half-century, Depardieu was a towering figure in French cinema, known for his commanding physical presence and versatility. In recent years, his behavior toward women has come under renewed scrutiny, including after a documentary showed him repeatedly making obscene remarks and gestures during a 2018 trip to North Korea.

articles.title: Ashes of exiled Nobel Laureate Miguel Ángel Asturias returned to Guatemala
articles.summary: The poet, writer and diplomat died in Europe in 1974 having been forced to leave his native country.
articles.body:
The remains of writer and diplomat Miguel Ángel Asturias have been buried in his native Guatemala 52 years after he died in exile.

His ashes were brought to Guatemala from Paris, where he had lived before his death from cancer in the Spanish capital, Madrid, in 1974.

Asturias was awarded the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1967 for his vivid writings, which drew on the experiences of indigenous Guatemalans.

The urn containing his ashes was placed in soil gathered from different parts of Guatemala at a cultural centre named after him in Guatemala City.

His son, whose name is also Miguel Ángel Asturias, said at the ceremony on Sunday: "I can tell you, old man, that you are with us, you are in your homeland, you will sleep beneath your own skies."

Asturias, who was born in 1899, first moved to Paris in the 1920s to study ethnology.

Influenced by the surrealists, he wrote his first major work, Legends of Guatemala, a retelling of Maya origin legends and mythological tales, while in France.

Subsequent works, such as the 1946 novel The President and his Banana Trilogy, denounced the terrors of dictatorship in Latin America and the exploitation indigenous workers suffered on banana plantations.

Arguably his most famous novel was Men of Maize, published in 1949, which explores the struggles of indigenous communities as the world around them quickly changes and modernises.

Between 1944 and 1954, a period known as "Guatemala's 10 Years of Spring", he served in several diplomatic posts in Central and South America and continued writing.

But when the democratically elected Guatemalan President Jacobo Árbenz Guzmán was deposed in a CIA-backed coup in 1954, Asturias was stripped of his Guatemalan citizenship, his books were banned and he had to go into exile.

At Sunday's burial ceremony, Asturias's son said that the writer had "always wanted to be in Guatemala" but "political conditions did not allow him to".

The family only agreed to have the ashes moved from Père Lachaise cemetery in Paris to Guatemala after the current progressive president of Guatemala, Bernardo Arévalo, was elected in 2023.

Arévalo praised Asturias at the interment ceremony as "our voice in the world".

"He deserved to rest in the land he named and reinvented in his pages," said Arévalo, whose father Juan José appointed Asturias to the diplomatic service when the older Arévalo served as president during the 10 Year Spring.

articles.title: Russian attacks kill three in Ukraine, EU accuses Moscow of prolonging war
articles.summary: EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas says Russian President Vladimir Putin is making maximalist demands.
articles.body:
Russian attacks have killed at least three people in Ukraine, as the European Union accuses Moscow of stalling talks aimed at ending the war.

Russia carried out several attacks on Monday, including in the village of Sadove in southern Ukraine’s Kherson region, killing a man on a moped, according to Governor Oleksandr Prokudin.

Another person was killed in a Russian attack in Dnipro city in central Ukraine, according to Oleksandr Hanzha, the head of the Dnipropetrovsk region’s military administration.

Elsewhere, a 59-year-old man was killed in a Russian drone attack in the village of Bilenke in the southern region of Zaporizhia, said Mykhailo Semikin, the acting head of the region’s military administration.

Monday’s attacks come as EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs Kaja Kallas accused Russian President Vladimir Putin of making maximalist demands in a bid to extend the conflict.

After negotiations in Abu Dhabi last week, the United States encouraged Ukraine and its backers to agree to a Russian demand for a new security framework for Europe, suggesting that it might help bring peace.

But the Europeans see that as a Russian attempt to weaken NATO by obliging the military alliance to pull troops and equipment back westward, similar to the way they were deployed before the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland joined in 1999.

“In 2021, Russia’s demands were a pretext for war. In 2026, they are pretext to keep the war going,” Kallas said in a post on X.

“A ceasefire must come first. It must be the basis to start the talks about anything else. With EU Foreign Ministers, we will discuss our own demands on Moscow to reply to the maximum demands that Russia is presenting.”

Meanwhile, Ukrainian drone attacks in the Belgorod region of southwest Russia killed one person on Monday, local authorities said.

The Russian Defence Ministry said on Monday that it had intercepted 1,336 drones during overnight attacks by Ukraine.

Kyiv received $1.88bn from the European Commission on Monday to buy drones, ammunition and air ⁠defence systems. The money is part of a larger $99bn loan approved in February. Separately, the EU approved its largest-ever single payment to Ukraine, about $8.7bn.

“Thank you to [the] EU Commission and EU Council for approving the largest-ever single payment to Ukraine under the Ukraine Facility, amounting to nearly €8 billion [$8.7bn],” Zelenskyy said in a post on X.

“I thank President Von Der leyen for her personal efforts to expedite the preparation of this payment, given Ukraine’s growing budgetary needs ahead of winter and intensified Russian attacks on our energy, heating, water supply, and other critical infrastructure.”

The EU is currently pushing for a ceasefire followed by a lasting peace agreement to end the four-and-a-half-year conflict.

The bloc on Monday imposed more sanctions on Russia, targeting nearly 50 banks and financial institutions. Several businesspeople with links to the energy sector, the trade in oil, and petroleum products were also sanctioned.

Dozens of others accused of spreading pro-Russian propaganda and disinformation were also hit with travel bans and asset freezes.

Last week, two days of talks between Russian and Ukrainian officials were held in the United Arab Emirates.

The discussions were mediated by the US and led to an agreement on a prisoner exchange. However, they failed to make a breakthrough on ending the war.

articles.title: Willie Geist Announces Departure From MS NOW for Expanded Role at TODAY
articles.summary: Willie Geist announced he’s leaving “Morning Joe” at the end of the year to work full-time at NBC News and focus on Sunday TODAY.
articles.body: For the past year, Willie Geist has worked for two networks in two studios across Midtown. Now he’s down to one. He’ll sign off from MS NOW’s “Morning Joe” in December, after nearly two decades on the show, for an expanded role at NBC News and focus on Sunday TODAY. Willie shared the news on Nov. 16 on “Morning Joe, which he has co-hosted since it launched in 2007. “It was never intended to last forever,” he said about working at two networks. He explained that there had been an informal understanding that he would stay at MS NOW, formerly MSNBC, through the midterm elections. He told co-hosts Joe Scarborough and Mika Brzezinski that nearly 20 years beside them has been “the joy of a lifetime, the job of a lifetime.” In his new role he will also appear more often on TODAY and across NBC News platforms. “I am so grateful to both NBC and MS NOW for the unique opportunity to do what I love at both networks,” Willie said in a statement. “This is a bittersweet goodbye to Joe, Mika, and the place that made possible everything else in my career over the last two decades, but I am thrilled to settle in with my family at TODAY and dedicate all of my time to that special place.” When Comcast officially spun off some cable networks from NBCUniversal in January, Willie became the only on-air personality working for both NBC News and Versant’s MS NOW. Since then he has gone back and forth between the “Morning Joe” studios in Times Square and TODAY’s home at Rockefeller Center. Willie joined TODAY in 2012 as co-host of the 9 a.m. hour and took over Sunday TODAY in 2016. Since then the show has won two Murrow Awards and become a place where some of the biggest stars in the world sit down for in-depth conversations. His Sunday Sitdown guests have included Dolly Parton, Paul McCartney, the Rolling Stones, Bad Bunny, Al Pacino, Steph Curry and David Letterman. In 2025 he started doing those interviews in front of a crowd. Sunday Sitdown Live has played New York and Nashville with guests like comedian Nate Bargatze, Ryan Reynolds, Luke Combs, Ina Garten and stand-up Jim Gaffigan. Willie has won an Emmy. He also hosts the Sunday Sitdown podcast and contributes to NBC Sports. Sunday TODAY with Willie Geist airs Sunday mornings on NBC.

articles.title: Georgia O’Keeffe painting found in NY closet set to sell for more than $3 million
articles.summary: A Georgia O’Keeffe painting that had been stashed in a New York City closet since the 1980s is expected to fetch more than $3 million when it goes up for auction this week.
articles.body: The painting was buried behind coats and boxes in the closet of a Manhattan apartment for decades. Few if anyone knew about the hidden treasure until the woman in her 90s who lived there nonchalantly told her niece one day, “oh, by the way, there’s a Georgia O’Keeffe in the closet.” The painting — an early example from a time when O’Keeffe became enamored with the American Southwest — depicts a classic New Mexico landscape with rolling hills in earth tones. Christie’s estimates its value at $3 to $5 million. It is set to go up for auction on Tuesday. The auction house says the painting from 1930 was likely the first in a series of three. The second is in New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art. The other, for many years, was in the collection of the Rockefeller family. Up until now, the whereabouts of the first one had largely been a mystery. O’Keeffe painting comes from a key period The painting of Lobo Peak near Taos, New Mexico, is “particularly important because of its early date and its representation of the inception point of O’Keeffe’s time in the American Southwest,” said Tylee Abbott, director of American Art at Christie’s. In 1963, a New York art gallery sold the painting for $3,800 to a woman who gave it to her daughter. “Before that it was only known through photography that had been taken in 1931,” Abbott said. O’Keeffe, who died in 1986 at age 98, is often called the “Mother of American modernism.” She was a pioneer with her own style of abstract art, most known for paintings of flowers and Southwestern landscapes. She lived in Abiquiu, New Mexico, where she built a home and studio on land with breathtaking desert vistas that inspired the work of the 20th century painter. Many Native American communities trace their ancestry to the area in northern New Mexico. Family believes painting was a graduation gift The daughter of the woman who purchased the painting in 1963 kept it at her apartment in New York’s East Village, the auction house said. The family has asked the auction house not to release their identities. But they did share with Christie’s some details, including how the artwork was found. The woman who owned the painting lived into her late 90s before dying recently. Never married, she was extremely private and incredibly smart, the family said. At one point in her life, she worked with the US Foreign Service, spending time in Europe. She collected antiques and abstract art but nothing close to the stature of the O’Keeffe. The family believes she received the painting as a graduation gift from her mother after earning a master’s degree in the 1960s. For many years, she displayed it until the mid-’80s when she noticed a guest looking at it a little too closely. Painting has O’Keeffe’s signature mark She boxed it back into the original packing crate and put it in the back of a closet, said her niece, who spent the last few years caring for her and spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity to honor the family’s request for privacy. Around 2022, the woman first mentioned to her niece that the painting was in the front closet. It stayed there until this year when they were cleaning out the apartment and getting her affairs in order. Once unboxed, it was obvious the painting was authentic. It has all the hallmarks of O’Keeffe’s work — including her signature marking on the back, a star with her initials “OK” scrawled in the middle.

articles.title: Hillary Clinton: Carney ‘maybe’ now ‘leader of the free world’
articles.summary: Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton said that Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is “maybe” the “leader of the free world.” During an event in New York City last Tuesday that was broadcast on MS NOW over the weekend, the outlet’s Rachel Maddow asked Clinton if she believed “that there is a leader of the…
articles.body:
Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton said that Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is “maybe” the “leader of the free world.”

During an event in New York City last Tuesday that was broadcast on MS NOW over the weekend, the outlet’s Rachel Maddow asked Clinton if she believed “that there is a leader of the free world right now.”

The former senator and first lady later added that “there are some good individual European leaders, but Europe has got to get itself organized so that, you know, the sum of the parts adds up to some kind of a whole, and be able to do a better job at making some tough decisions.”

In the last few years, Canada and the U.S., which are historical allies, have had tensions over President Trump’s tariff policy.

On Saturday , Carney said trade negotiations between Ottawa and Washington were moving forward amid a tariff battle that has stretched on for months.

The Canadian prime minister told reporters in Manila, Philippines, that he had talked with Trump, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, White House chief of staff Stephen Miller and other officials “just before” going to the Association of the Southeast Asian Nations’ (ASEAN) summit.

Carney also said he would not “settle for a deal” not in line with “a viable Canadian auto sector.”

“This is one of the fundamental issues in our trade negotiation, and we are making progress,” Carney said.

articles.title: WWE's Charlotte Flair reflects on Royal Rumble wins ahead of 2027 event, feels 'pressure' after making history

articles.body: Charlotte Flair has accrued an impressive list of accolades during her time in WWE. She’s a 14-time world champion, a Triple Crown champion and a Grand Slam champion. What is arguably more impressive than those feats is that she is the one and only two-time women’s Royal Rumble winner. She won the match in 2020 and defeated Rhea Ripley at WrestleMania 36 for the NXT Women’s Championship. In 2025, she won after coming all the way back from a devastating injury but fell short of capturing the title against Tiffany Stratton at WrestleMania 41. So, I was very nervous. Wasn't sure what the reception was gonna be, but knowing that I had crossed the finish lines in terms of when I was away, being back in that ring was all that I thought about. articles.title: 'Unmistakably' Sunderland artwork begins chiming
articles.summary: The new piece changes every hour and is on show in the city's Culture House for a year.
articles.body:
An artwork which changes every hour and aims to celebrate the identity of a city "on the brink of embracing a lot of change" has been officially unveiled.

Over the next year, Timepiece will see different 50-second long collages made from archive film, photos and audio chime on the hour through Sunderland's newly opened Culture House.

The piece, which was created by Jeremy Bradfield, Ben Lawrence and The Futureheads' Ross Millard, is one of the first major artworks to go on show at the venue.

Millard said Timepiece was "like a welcome for people" into the city, with each chime celebrating a different element of Sunderland's past, present and future.

The artwork was in the making for about a year.

Bradfield previously said he hoped the piece would "stir" a lot of memories.

The first chimes on Monday morning showcased glassblowing in the city and featured 1970s film material.

Millard, who created the soundtrack, said he had received a lot of messages from people saying they had enjoyed the artwork and were looking forward to "collecting" the 72 chimes.

"Sunderland is a city that's on the brink of embracing a lot of change," he said.

"And I think it's really nice to have something really familiar to people going on inside a building that is very sort of futuristic and forward-looking.

"If you're not from the city, I think when Timepiece comes on, it's so unmistakably of Sunderland, whether it's the coastal chimes with Roker Pier, and Cliff Park and the seafront, or it's the football chimes with either Roker Park or the Stadium of Light, there's so much that's obviously Sunderland in there that I'd like to think visitors will all catch on that quite quickly."

Themes include a 1950s bus ride through the city, the building and launching of a Hindustan Shipping Co ship at Doxford shipyard and glassblowing in the 1960s.

Bradfield said the oldest photo used in the artwork dated back to about 1913, with archive material provided by the University of Sunderland, The Bunker, Ashbrooke Sports Club, Friends of Roker Pier and Lighthouse, Ryhope Engine Museum, Sunderland Libraries and the North East Film Archive.

articles.title: Five EU countries unveil plans for Rwanda deportation hub
articles.summary: Five European countries on Monday unveiled plans to send rejected asylum seekers to a deportation hub in Rwanda, as centrist governments in Europe toughen immigration policies to counter growing public support for far-right parties.
articles.body: Five European countries on Monday unveiled plans to send rejected asylum seekers to a deportation hub in Rwanda, as centrist governments in Europe toughen immigration policies to counter growing public support for far-right parties. Germany, Austria, Greece, Denmark and the Netherlands have been working towards a deal for a so-called return hub for several months, part of a broader push inside the European Union to increase deportations and curb irregular migration. The five-country group was starting talks with Rwanda on setting up a deportation hub there, the Austrian government said in a statement on Monday. Negotiations should be quick so that the first deportations of rejected asylum seekers who cannot be sent back to their home countries can take place in 2027, Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker and his Danish counterpart Mette Frederiksen, added in a statement. The project, announced in Vienna, follows the approval of the EU’s new Return Regulation, designed to speed up deportations. “We are ready now to move into more concrete steps. I think it will be a game changer, making us able to confront the massive challenges of illegal migration,” Frederiksen told journalists in Vienna alongside Stocker, Rwanda’s interior minister and officials from the Netherlands, Greece and Germany. “We will take back control of our borders,” she added. With elections approaching in several EU countries and anti-immigration sentiment widespread, governments are under pressure to show they can control migration. Deportation hubs offer a highly visible demonstration of that resolve, analysts say. The scheme resembles Britain’s abandoned Rwanda deportation plan but differs in that it would only apply to migrants who have exhausted all legal avenues to remain in the European Union, rather than those whose claims are still being processed. Accountability questions Leaders from the five countries insist their plans will comply with EU and international law. But rights advocates have questioned whether migrants’ rights could be violated if they are transferred to a country they have no connection to. The Council of Europe, a pan-European human rights body, said in July that return hubs posed “considerable human rights risks.” In a joint statement, 45 rights, aid and trade union groups urged the five countries to abandon the Rwanda plan, saying neither legal safeguards nor monitoring mechanisms could eliminate the risk of rights abuses and that Rwanda fails to meet the human rights standards required under the EU’s new Return Regulation. “It signals that Member States accept the risk of serious human rights violations against one of the most marginalized groups in society, in return for a deterrence goal that evidence clearly suggests they will not reach,” the statement said. European officials backing the hubs say the policy’s main purpose is deterrence rather than large-scale removals. They argue the prospect of paying smugglers thousands of euros for a dangerous journey to Europe, only to be sent elsewhere, could dissuade some migrants from making the trip. Critics, however, say there is little evidence that tougher enforcement measures and deportation schemes reduce migration over the long term. “Enforcement changes how people travel, not whether they travel. Some pause or change route, and smugglers adapt and raise their prices,” said Roberto Forin of the Mixed Migration Centre, a research institute that collects data along migration routes. A willing host Rwanda has positioned itself as a destination for migrants whom Western countries want to remove, despite longstanding concerns about its own human rights record. Veteran President Paul Kagame won praise from Western and regional leaders for helping end Rwanda’s 1994 genocide and rebuilding the East African country into a destination for investment. However, critics accuse his government of suppressing dissent and supporting rebels alleged to have committed killings, rapes and other abuse in neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo. Rights advocates also point to restrictions on political freedoms and free speech. Freedom House rates it “Not Free” and cites what it describes as the suppression of political dissent through surveillance, intimidation, arbitrary detention and torture. The United States last year began transferring migrants to Rwanda under an agreement allowing it to deport up to 250 people. Britain abandoned its own plan to send asylum seekers to Rwanda after it was ruled unlawful by the country’s Supreme Court in 2023. Kigali sought a £50 million ($63.6 million) payment after the UK scheme was scrapped.
